Content:
Suppose we want to calculate the domain and range of [MATH: y = f(2x) -4.] To do this, we first sketch it by applying graph transformations, and then we read the domain and range from the graph of the transformed function.

Content:
To plot the graph of [MATH: y = f(2x) -4,] we apply the following steps:

Content:
- Take the curve [MATH: y=f(x).]
- Then, stretch the graph by a scale factor of [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}] parallel to the [MATH: x]-axis and get the graph of [MATH: y = f(2x).]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b5f1c5aa1de5667d9931744ead359799]

Content:
- Finally, we shift the result by [MATH: 4] units down and obtain the graph of [MATH: y = f(2x) -4.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/943cc2113d506ed2465f1d2f4123d3ca]

Content:
From here, we may deduce the following about the function [MATH: y=f(2x) -4\mathbin{:}]

Content:
- Its domain is [MATH: x\in (-3, 3].]
- For the range, we note the following:

- The minimum value is indicated by the [MATH: y]-coordinate of the point [MATH: (1, -7),] and this value is included in the range (since this point has a filled circle).
- The maximum value is indicated by the [MATH: y]-coordinate of the point [MATH: (-3,4),] and this value is not included in the range (since this point has an open circle).

Therefore, the range is [MATH: y\in [-7, 4).]

items.title: Finding the Domain of a Transformed Function

sections.normalized_html: The diagram above shows the graph of [MATH: y=f(x).] What is the domain of [MATH: y = f(2-x)?]
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/8d28fbaae7d6760efe0e1f517b516ff9]

The diagram above shows the graph of [MATH: y=f(x).] What is the domain of [MATH: y = f(2-x)?]

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's write the function in a form that is convenient for transformations:

[MATH: y = f(2-x) = f(-(x-2))]

When performing graph transformations, we must remember the following rule:

  1. First, we perform the transformations inside the argument of [MATH: f.] We first carry out horizontal stretches and reflections, followed by horizontal translations.

  2. Then, we perform the transformations outside the argument of [MATH: f.] We first carry out vertical stretches and reflections, followed by vertical translations.

So, to plot the graph of [MATH: y = f(-(x-2)),] we apply the following steps:

  • Take the curve [MATH: y=f(x).]

  • Then, reflect the graph across the [MATH: y]-axis and get the graph of [MATH: y = f(-x).]

  • Finally, we shift the result horizontally by [MATH: 2] units to the right and obtain the graph of [MATH: y = f(-(x-2)) .]

Therefore, the domain of [MATH: f(2-x)] is [MATH: [0,5).]
